codex: The grain that feeds the Sahel. It grows on rain that other crops call a drought.
description: a tall grass with a dense bottle-brush grain head

knowledgeLevels.1: Pearl millet. Tall grass, dense grain head like a bottle brush. This is food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: grain heads (thresh, winnow, grind). Stalks are fodder and building material.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the Sahel's staple grain — porridge, couscous, flatbread. Drought-tough; it fruits where maize dies.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest when heads are hard and dry; thresh by beating, winnow in wind. Pound to flour; stores a year dry. 2x yield if you cut whole heads before birds do.

lookalikeNote: The grain head is a dense cylindrical spike, unmistakable once headed. Young shoots resemble any grass — wait for the head.
name: Pearl Millet
preparation: Thresh and winnow the grain; grind to flour. Cook as porridge or couscous — raw grain is indigestible.
sources: field notes: dominant Sahel staple grain

uses.note: thresh, grind, cook as porridge/couscous

codex: Sorghum waits out the dry season in a granary and outlasts every other plan.
description: a tall cane-like grass with a loose branching head of grain

knowledgeLevels.1: Sorghum. Tall as a person, grain in a branching head. Food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: grain (thresh and grind), sweet stalks (chew for juice), leaves (fodder).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: porridge, flatbread, brewing. The grain keeps for years dry — famine insurance.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: some varieties have bitter tannin coats — taste a grain first; the sweet-stalk types are the treat. Harvest whole panicles; thresh dry.

lookalikeNote: Tall cane-like stalks with a loose branching grain head — distinct from pearl millet's dense spike. Wild sorghums exist; the grain head shape is the tell.
name: Sorghum
preparation: Thresh, winnow, grind. Cook thoroughly as porridge or flatbread.

uses.note: grain for porridge/flatbread; sweet stalks chewed fresh

codex: The oldest cultivated grain in West Africa, and the fastest from seed to bowl.
description: a delicate low grass with tiny grains on finger-like heads

knowledgeLevels.1: Fonio. Small grass, tiny grains. The grains are food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the tiny grains (pound to dehusk, winnow). Cooks in minutes.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: West Africa's ancient grain — porridge, couscous. Matures fast; the hungry-season bridge.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the grains are sand-sized — winnow carefully or you eat grit. Parboil then steam; 2x yield from a patient threshing.

lookalikeNote: Tiny grains on delicate finger-like seed heads. Resembles wild Digitaria grasses — the cultivated stands are planted in rows; wild ones scatter.
name: Fonio
preparation: Dehusk by pounding, winnow well, rinse. Cooks fast — porridge or steamed like couscous.
sources: field notes: West African Sahel grain

uses.note: dehusked grains cooked as porridge or couscous

codex: Beans for the grain, leaves for the pot — the vine that completes the millet.
description: a trailing vine with three-part leaves and long thin pods

knowledgeLevels.1: Cowpea. Vine, three-part leaves, long pods. The beans inside are food — cooked.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: dried beans (boil well), young leaves (greens), fresh pods (vegetable).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: protein to go with the grain — the Sahel's bean. Fixes nitrogen; planted with the millet.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: beans must be boiled until fully soft — undercooked beans punish you. Young leaves are the fastest green you'll get.

lookalikeNote: Climbing/trailing vine with trifoliate leaves and long thin pods. Pods resemble wild legumes — the plump cultivated pods are the tell.
name: Cowpea
preparation: Boil dried beans until completely soft. Never eat dried beans raw or undercooked.

uses.note: beans boiled soft; young leaves as greens

codex: Called groundnut here, peanut elsewhere. Fat you can carry in your pocket.
description: a low bushy plant with paired oval leaves; nuts underground

knowledgeLevels.1: Groundnut. Low bush, nuts buried under it. Dig them up.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the nuts (roast or boil). Oil-rich — serious calories.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: roast for eating, pound for sauce, press for oil. Protein and fat together.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: NEVER eat moldy, shriveled, or bitter nuts — aflatoxin from bad storage is a slow poison. Roast fresh nuts; discard anything off-smelling.

lookalikeNote: Low bushy plant with paired oval leaflets; the nuts grow underground. Dig carefully — the shells are unmistakable, but moldy nuts are the real danger.
name: Peanut
preparation: Roast or boil fresh nuts. Discard any moldy, discolored, or bitter nuts — aflatoxin.
sources: field notes: aflatoxin risk in Sahel storage

uses.note: nuts roasted or boiled; pounded into sauce

codex: The tree of life, and it earns the name. Fruit in the hungry season, leaves for the pot, shade for the village.
description: a massive bottle-trunked tree, branches like roots against the sky

knowledgeLevels.1: Baobab. The upside-down tree. Everything it offers is food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: dry fruit pulp (tangy, vitamin C — eat dry or stir into water), young leaves (greens, cooked), seeds (roast).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the fruit is called monkey bread — powdery pulp eaten as-is or as a drink. Leaves make a mucilaginous sauce leaf. Vitamin C when nothing else has any.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: fruit ripens in the dry season — the hungry months. Crack the hard pod, shake out the dry pulp; no cooking needed. Leaves dried and pounded keep for the dry season.

lookalikeNote: Unmistakable: a trunk like a water tower, branches like roots in the air. Nothing else looks like it.
name: Baobab
preparation: Eat the dry fruit pulp as-is or stirred into water. Cook young leaves as greens.

uses.note: dry fruit pulp eaten raw or as drink; leaves cooked as greens
vitamin C — scurvy prevention in the dry season

codex: Sour enough to wake the dead, sweet enough to keep you walking. The traveler's tree.
description: a broad shady tree with feathery leaves and hanging brown pods

knowledgeLevels.1: Tamarind. Big shady tree, brown pods. The sour pulp inside is food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe pod pulp (sour-sweet, eat fresh or soak into a drink), seeds (roast in famine).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: souring for sauces, a tart drink, travel food — the pulp keeps for months. Vitamin C and appetite when food is dull.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pick pods that are brown and brittle; the pulp should pull away clean. Soak pulp, strain seeds — the drink keeps days.

lookalikeNote: Feathery compound leaves, brown curved pods hanging in clusters. The sour pulp inside is the tell — nothing poisonous mimics it.
name: Tamarind
preparation: Eat ripe pulp fresh or soak in water for a tart drink. Strain out seeds and fibers.

uses.note: ripe pulp eaten fresh or as a drink

codex: Sweet underground nuts that survive the dry season in the ground, waiting.
description: a grass-like sedge; striped nutty tubers underground

knowledgeLevels.1: Tiger nut. Sedge, tubers underground. Dig — the striped tubers are food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the tubers (eat fresh, dried, or ground into a sweet milky drink).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: sweet, chewy, filling — the original energy bar. The drink (kunun aya) is a meal in a cup.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: wash tubers well — grit is the enemy. Dry them for storage; soak dried ones overnight before eating.

lookalikeNote: Grass-like sedge with triangular stems; the tubers are small striped nuts underground. Other sedges look identical above ground — dig to confirm.
name: Tiger Nut
preparation: Wash well. Eat fresh, dried, or ground and soaked into a sweet drink.

uses.note: tubers fresh, dried, or as a ground drink

codex: The pod that holds a sauce together. Slimy is the point.
description: a hibiscus-like plant with ridged green pods

knowledgeLevels.1: Okra. Ridged green pods. Pick young pods — food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: young pods (cook), leaves (greens), seeds (roast as coffee substitute in famine).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the pod's mucilage thickens sauces — the base of a thousand Sahel stews. Leaves are good greens.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pick pods young and tender; old pods are woody string. Slice and sun-dry for the dry season.

lookalikeNote: Ridged green pods on a hibiscus-like plant. WARNING: thorn-apple (Datura) grows nearby with spiky round pods — compare carefully; okra pods are ridged and elongated, never round and spiny.
name: Okra
preparation: Cook young pods — stews, sauces. Sun-dry sliced pods for storage.

uses.note: young pods cooked; leaves as greens

codex: Red as sunset, sour as gossip. The drink of every market in the Sahel.
description: a tall plant with deep red fleshy calyces

knowledgeLevels.1: Bissap. Red fleshy cups around the seed pods. Those red calyces are food and drink.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: calyces (steep into tart red tea, hot or cold), leaves (sour greens).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: bissap — the Sahel's drink. Vitamin C, cooling, keeps in the heat. Leaves sour a sauce like tamarind.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest calyces when plump and deep red; dry them — dried bissap keeps a year and is trade goods.

lookalikeNote: Deep red fleshy calyces around a seed pod — unmistakable when fruiting. Leaves resemble okra's; the red calyx is the confirmation.
name: Bissap Hibiscus
preparation: Steep fresh or dried calyces in water for bissap tea. Cook leaves as sour greens.
sources: field notes: bissap is the Sahel's drink

uses.note: calyces as tea; leaves as sour greens
vitamin C; cooling drink in heat

codex: The tree that feeds you twice — leaves in the rains, pods in the dry.
description: a slender fast-growing tree with feathery leaves and long hanging pods

knowledgeLevels.1: Moringa. Feathery leaves, long pods. The leaves are food — fresh or dried.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: leaves (eat fresh, cooked, or dried and pounded to powder), pods (cook young), flowers (tea).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the most nutritious leaf in the Sahel — protein, iron, vitamins. Dried leaf powder keeps months and fortifies porridge.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: strip leaves, dry in shade (sun kills the vitamins), pound to powder. A spoonful a day in the hungry season.

lookalikeNote: Feathery twice-divided leaves, slender trunk, long ribbed pods. The drumstick pods are the tell.
name: Moringa
preparation: Eat leaves fresh or cooked; dry and pound to powder for storage. Cook young pods.

uses.note: leaves fresh/cooked/dried; young pods cooked
iron, vitamin A — deficiency greens

codex: Gold you have to work for. The nuts are useless raw; the butter feeds a continent.
description: a broad gnarled tree with round green fruits

knowledgeLevels.1: Shea. Gnarled tree, round fruits. The nuts inside need work before they're food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: nuts (process to butter — never eat raw), fruit pulp (eat fresh when ripe, sweet).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: shea butter — cooking fat, the Sahel's oil. The ripe fruit pulp is a sweet snack in season.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: boil nuts, sun-dry, crack, roast kernels, grind, knead with water — the butter rises. Days of work; months of fat.

lookalikeNote: Broad gnarled canopy, round green fruits ripening in the rains. The fruit pulp is sweet and safe fresh — the NUT is the part that needs processing.
name: Shea
preparation: NEVER eat raw nuts. Boil, dry, crack, roast, grind, knead — extract the butter. Eat ripe fruit pulp fresh.
sources: field notes: shea parklands, women's harvest

uses.note: nuts processed to butter; ripe fruit pulp eaten fresh

codex: Sweet, bitter, and stubborn — the tree that fruits when nothing else dares.
description: a spiny evergreen tree with plum-sized yellow-brown fruits

knowledgeLevels.1: Desert date. Spiny tree, plum-sized fruits. The ripe pulp is food — bittersweet.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe fruit pulp (eat fresh or dried), young leaves (boil as vegetable), kernel (crack the stone, roast — oily).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: pulp is candy in the dry season; kernel oil cooks and the kernel meal feeds stock. Leaves are famine greens.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: ripe = yellow-brown and fragrant; green fruit is harsh. Soak fruit, wash off pulp, sun-dry the stones, crack for kernels — stone-on-stone work.

lookalikeNote: Spiny branches, plum-sized faintly five-grooved fruits ripening yellow-brown. Green fruit is harsh — wait for the color change.
name: Desert Date
preparation: Eat ripe pulp fresh or dried. Boil young leaves. Crack stones for kernels; roast them.
sources: MDPI Foods 2023 — Balanites aegyptiaca kernel oil (Sahel/Sahara uses)

uses.note: ripe pulp fresh/dried; leaves boiled; kernels roasted
pulp used traditionally for cough, constipation

codex: The bush by every path, fruiting in the worst months. The Sahel's candy store.
description: a thorny bush with small round yellow-red fruits

knowledgeLevels.1: Jujube. Thorny bush, small round fruits. Ripe ones are food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe fruits (eat fresh, dry for later), leaves (fodder, tea).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: sweet-tart snack, dried into a travel food. Fruits in the dry season when little else does.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pick when deep yellow to red and slightly wrinkled — fully ripe. Dry in the sun; dried jujubes keep months.

lookalikeNote: Thorny zigzag branches, small round fruits ripening yellow to red. Ripe fruit is safe; unripe green ones are just sour, not dangerous.
name: Jujube
preparation: Eat ripe fruit fresh or sun-dried.

uses.note: ripe fruits fresh or dried

codex: Small white berries on a dusty bush — the children's harvest.
description: a dusty grey-green bush with small white-pink berries

knowledgeLevels.1: Grewia. Grey-green bush, small pale berries. The ripe berries are food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe berries (eat fresh; pound with water into a drink), leaves (famine greens).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: called godeim — the berries make a sweet drink; children live on them in season. Iron-rich.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: berries ripen white to pinkish — taste for sweetness. Pound, soak, strain; the juice is the prize.

lookalikeNote: Small shrub with rough grey-green leaves and pea-sized pale berries. Ripe berries are sweet — sour or bitter ones aren't ready.
name: White Crossberry
preparation: Eat ripe berries fresh or pounded into a drink.
sources: Sudan National Food Research Centre — indigenous fruits (godeim)

uses.note: ripe berries fresh or as a drink

codex: The weed that feeds. It volunteers in every disturbed patch of ground.
description: a fast leafy green, sometimes reddish stems

knowledgeLevels.1: Amaranth. Leafy green, fast-growing. The young leaves are food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: young leaves and shoots (cook as greens), seeds (grain — thresh like millet, smaller).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: alefu — the everyday green. Iron and protein when the grain runs thin. Seeds are a bonus grain.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pick young tops before flowering; older leaves get tough. The seeds ripen after the leaves are done — two harvests, one plant.

lookalikeNote: Fast-growing leafy green with a dense flower spike. Young plants resemble other weeds — the grain-like seed head at maturity confirms it.
name: African Amaranth
preparation: Cook young leaves as greens. Thresh seeds as a grain.

uses.note: young leaves cooked; seeds as grain

codex: Tree tears you can eat. The Sahel's oldest export is food if you know which wound to tap.
description: a thorny acacia; amber gum oozing from bark wounds

knowledgeLevels.1: Gum acacia. Thorny tree, amber tears on the bark. The gum is food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: gum tears (dissolve in water — a sustaining drink), seeds (famine food, cooked), pods (fodder).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: gum arabic — dissolved, it's calories and calm for an empty stomach. A handful of gum and water is a meal's ghost.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: collect tears that are hard and clear; tap by wounding bark in the dry season and return in days. The pale tears are the cleanest.

lookalikeNote: Thorny acacia with paired white thorns; amber gum tears on wounded bark. Other acacias gum too — the pale hard tears of this one are the food grade.
name: Gum Acacia
preparation: Dissolve clean gum tears in water as a drink. Cook seeds in famine.

uses.note: gum dissolved in water; seeds cooked in famine

codex: Medicine with teeth. It cures at a spoonful and punishes at a bowlful.
description: a fast tree with feathery leaves and bitter smell

knowledgeLevels.1: Neem. Feathery leaves, bitter smell. Medicine, not food — small amounts only.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: leaves and bark (bitter tea — fever, malaria tradition), twigs (chewing sticks), seeds (oil — NOT food).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the Sahel's pharmacy tree — fever tea, wound wash, tooth sticks. The bitterness is the dose talking.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: a small handful of leaves steeped, not boiled to death. Large doses of leaves or any seed oil are toxic — this is a medicine with a ceiling.

lookalikeNote: Feathery compound leaves with a bitter garlic-onion smell when crushed, small white flowers, olive-like fruits. The bitter smell is the tell — moringa, which looks similar, smells like nothing.
name: Neem
preparation: Steep a small handful of leaves as a bitter tea. Never ingest seed oil. Chew twigs as tooth sticks.

uses.note: bitter leaf tea for fever; twigs as tooth sticks

codex: A palm that fruits where the groundwater runs, and feeds the villages along the river.
description: a clustering palm with orange date-like fruits

knowledgeLevels.1: Senegal date palm. Clustering palm, orange fruits. The ripe fruits are food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe fruits (eat fresh — sweet pulp around a hard seed), palm heart (famine food, kills the stem), young shoots (vegetable).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the wild date of the riverbanks — sweet, filling, reliable. The heart is a last-resort meal; taking it kills that stem.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: fruits ripen orange and soft; green ones are astringent. Clusters keep on the tree for weeks — harvest as needed.

lookalikeNote: Clustering palm (many stems) with feathery fronds and orange date clusters. Green unripe fruits are astringent but not dangerous — wait for orange.
name: Senegal Date Palm
preparation: Eat ripe orange fruits fresh. Cook young shoots as vegetable.

uses.note: ripe fruits fresh; young shoots as vegetable

codex: Gingerbread you have to gnaw. The doum fruits when the river remembers it.
description: a forked palm with fan leaves and large brown gingerbread-smelling fruits

knowledgeLevels.1: Doum palm. Forked trunk, fan leaves. The brown fruits are food — gnaw the rind.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: fruit rind (gnaw the sweet fibrous flesh; soak pounded rind for a sweet drink), unripe kernel (crack green fruit for the white nut), germinated shoots (vegetable).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the gingerbread tree — the rind tastes of spice and honey. Pounded rind soaked in water makes a brown sweet juice for millet cakes.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: green fruit hides a white edible kernel — crack it young. Ripe fruit: chew the rind, spit the fiber, or pound and soak for juice. The hard seed is vegetable ivory, not food.

lookalikeNote: The only palm that forks — Y-shaped trunk, fan leaves. Large brown woody fruits. Unmistakable.
name: Doum Palm
preparation: Gnaw ripe rind; pound rind and soak for sweet juice. Crack green fruit for the white kernel.

uses.note: rind gnawed or soaked for juice; green kernels

codex: The melon is a lie; the seeds are the truth. Bitter enough to kill, rich enough to live on.
description: a trailing vine with yellow-green melon-sized fruits

knowledgeLevels.1: Egusi melon. Vine, melon-sized fruits. The FRUIT is poison-bitter — the SEEDS are food, cooked.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: seeds (separate from the pulp, wash, roast or boil well — the famous egusi). The flesh is violently bitter and purgative.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: egusi soup — the seeds ground into a rich thick soup, protein and oil. Famine food of the Sahara for millennia.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest ripe, crack, scoop seeds, wash them free of pulp, sun-dry, then roast. The bitter flesh never goes in the pot — not a scrap.

lookalikeNote: Looks EXACTLY like a small watermelon — yellow-green rind, melon size. Taste a crumb of flesh: watermelon is sweet, egusi is unspeakably bitter. The bitterness is the warning. Never confuse the two.
name: Egusi Melon
preparation: Separate seeds from bitter pulp; wash, dry, roast or boil thoroughly. Never eat the flesh.
sources: Wikipedia — Citrullus colocynthis (culinary: seeds separated and thoroughly cooked)
phys.org 2022 — ancient egusi seed use, Libya/Sudan

uses.note: seeds washed and cooked — egusi soup base

codex: Bitter as regret, good as medicine. The washing is the cooking.
description: a shrub with dark green slightly bitter-smelling leaves

knowledgeLevels.1: Bitter leaf. Shrub, dark leaves. The leaves are food — but only after washing the bitter out.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: leaves (squeeze-wash repeatedly, then boil — the classic soup leaf).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the great West African soup leaf — nutrition under the bitterness. Also a fever tea in small amounts.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pound or squeeze the leaves in water, change the water, repeat until the bitterness is bearable. Boil after washing. Under-washed leaves are a stomach ache, not a meal.

lookalikeNote: Shrub with dark green elliptical leaves, intensely bitter when crushed. The bitterness itself is the ID — sweet lookalikes don't punish you for skipping the wash.
name: Bitter Leaf
preparation: Squeeze-wash leaves in several changes of water, then boil. Never eat unwashed.
sources: Frontiers in Natural Products 2024 — Vernonia amygdalina review
European J. Food Sci. Tech. — debittering methods

uses.note: leaves squeeze-washed and boiled
fever tea, small amounts

codex: The root that feeds half a billion people — and poisons anyone in a hurry.
description: a woody shrub with starchy tuberous roots

knowledgeLevels.1: Cassava. Shrub, thick roots. The roots are food ONLY after proper processing.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: roots (peel completely, soak/ferment, then cook thoroughly). Leaves (boil well — also cyanogenic raw).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the calorie backbone — garri, fufu, éba. But bitter varieties carry cyanide; the processing is not optional.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: peel all skin, soak peeled roots in water (change it), ferment sour, then roast or boil. Sweet varieties need peeling + thorough cooking; bitter ones need the full soak-ferment. Hungry shortcuts have killed people — WHO counts ~200 deaths a year from bad processing.

lookalikeNote: Woody shrub with palmate leaves and thick roots. Sweet vs bitter varieties look identical — treat every root as bitter until you know the planting. The rule is the processing, not the variety.
name: Cassava
preparation: Peel completely, soak/ferment in changed water, then cook thoroughly. Never eat raw or under-processed.

uses.note: roots peeled, soaked/fermented, cooked — garri/fufu

codex: Pound it and it becomes a meal you can hold. The yam barn is the bank.
description: a climbing vine with large starchy tubers underground

knowledgeLevels.1: Yam. Climbing vine, huge tubers. The tubers are food — cooked.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: tubers (boil, roast, or pound into fufu). Never raw — raw yam is harsh and some wild kinds are toxic.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: pounded yam — the feast food. Roasted yam is travel food. A barn of yams is wealth you can eat.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest by digging carefully — broken tubers rot. Cure in shade; store in an airy barn. Boil or roast fully; pounding is for the celebration.

lookalikeNote: Climbing vine with heart-shaped leaves and massive tubers. Cultivated yams are the food — wild yams in the bush can be bitter and toxic; don't dig at random.
name: White Yam
preparation: Boil, roast, or pound fully cooked. Never eat raw.

uses.note: tubers boiled/roasted/pounded

codex: The lily that feeds the floodplain. Roots in the mud, dinner on the plate.
description: broad floating leaves and white-blue flowers on still water

knowledgeLevels.1: Water lily. Floating leaves, showy flowers. The tubers and seeds are food — cooked.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: rhizomes/tubers (dig from mud, boil), seeds (dry, grind or pop like grain).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: floodplain food — tubers when the water drops, seeds when it flowers. Filling starch.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: feel for tubers in the mud with your feet; boil well. Dry seeds fully before grinding.

lookalikeNote: Floating round leaves with a notch, white to blue flowers. The edible tubers are underwater — confirm by digging, not by the flower.
name: Water Lily
preparation: Boil tubers from the mud. Dry and grind seeds.

uses.note: tubers boiled; seeds dried and ground

codex: Rice's wild ancestor, still feeding the floodplains it came from.
description: a tall wild grass with rice-like grains, standing in shallow water

knowledgeLevels.1: Wild rice. Tall grass in shallow water, rice-like grains. The grains are food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: grains (knock into a canoe or basket, winnow, parch, cook).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the Niger floodplain's grain — harvested from boats by knocking ripe heads. Nutty, filling, free.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest by bending heads over a basket and beating — the ripe grains fall. Parch to loosen husks, winnow, then cook like rice. Shallow water only; deep water is for fish.

lookalikeNote: Tall grass in standing water with rice-like panicles. Resembles cultivated rice — the wild stands are in natural floodplain, unplanted rows.
name: African Wild Rice
preparation: Knock ripe grains into a basket, winnow, parch, cook.
sources: field notes: Niger inner delta grain

uses.note: grains knocked, winnowed, parched, cooked

codex: The famine berry. Bitter, small, and there when nothing else is.
description: a tough evergreen shrub with small round berries

knowledgeLevels.1: Hanza. Tough shrub, small round berries. The ripe berries are famine food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: berries (soak to remove bitterness, then eat or dry), leaves (famine greens, cooked).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: called hanza — the berries carry villages through the hungry season. Bitter raw; soaking tames them.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: soak berries in several changes of water to debitter, then dry. The bitterness is the price of a free harvest.

lookalikeNote: Evergreen shrub with small round green-to-yellow berries. Bitter when raw — the soaking is the preparation, not a warning sign of poison.
name: Hanza
preparation: Soak berries in changed water to debitter, then eat or dry.

uses.note: berries soaked to debitter, eaten or dried

codex: Pretty as an apple, honest as a lie. Everything about it is poison.
description: a grey-green shrub with apple-sized green fruits and milky sap

knowledgeLevels.1: Sodom apple. Grey-green shrub, apple-sized green fruits. DO NOT EAT. The sap burns.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: none are food. The milky latex blisters skin and blinds eyes; the fruit's cardiac poisons stop hearts.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none for the pot. Traditional medicine uses it in expert hands only — the margin between dose and death is a whisper.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: recognize it at a glance — thick grey-green leaves, inflated apple-like green fruits, white latex from any cut. Teach everyone. This is the plant that kills the curious.

lookalikeNote: THIS IS THE LOOKALIKE WARNING: the green apple-sized fruits look like food from a distance. They are not. Milky latex from any cut = walk away. Nothing edible in the Sahel bleeds white like this.
name: Sodom Apple
preparation: No preparation makes it food. Avoid entirely.
sources: PMC — ocular toxicity of Calotropis latex

codex: The living fence with murder in its seeds. One to three seeds hospitalize; children die.
description: a small tree with lobed leaves and black seeds in three-part pods

knowledgeLevels.1: Physic nut. Small tree, often planted as a living fence. The seeds are POISON.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: none are food. Seeds carry curcin and phorbol esters — 1–3 seeds poison an adult, fewer kill a child.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none for the pot. The oil burns in lamps and runs engines; the seed cake kills rats. That is its job.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the living fences around fields are physic nut — teach children by name. The black seeds look like small chestnuts; the resemblance is the trap.

lookalikeNote: Planted in rows as living fences — lobed leaves, yellow-green three-part fruits, black seeds. The seeds look like small edible chestnuts. They are not. Fence rows = warning rows.
name: Physic Nut
preparation: No preparation makes it food. Avoid entirely.
sources: FAO — Jatropha curcas toxicity (1-3 seeds toxic)

codex: The trumpet flower that unmakes minds. Beautiful, common, and utterly not food.
description: a weed with trumpet flowers and spiny round pods

knowledgeLevels.1: Thorn apple. Trumpet flowers, spiny round pods. POISON — every part.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: none are food. Tropane alkaloids — delirium, racing heart, death. The seeds are the worst.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none for the pot. This is the plant that steals minds; there is no safe dose for the hungry.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the spiny round pods grow near okra fields and look vaguely like okra's cousins. They are not cousins. Okra pods are ridged and elongated; thorn-apple pods are round and spiny. When in doubt, the trumpet flower decides — walk away.

lookalikeNote: CRITICAL LOOKALIKE: spiny round pods vs okra's ridged elongated pods. Same fields, same season. Check the pod shape, check for the trumpet flower. A mistake here is a funeral.
name: Thorn Apple
preparation: No preparation makes it food. Avoid entirely.
